title: Landing UX: Voice Layering & Trust Playbook
body:
Purpose and scope:

This is a lightweight playbook for homepage and product landing copy that prioritizes technical credibility for engineering buyers while preserving a concise, action-oriented marketing funnel for broader PM/Founders personas. Use this doc to: iterate hero variants, define microcopy patterns for trust signals, and scope A/B experiments with measurable success criteria.

Audience slices (primary -> secondary):
- Primary: backend/platform/ML engineers evaluating inference for production (care about SLOs, versioning, latency percentiles, and predictable unit costs)
- Secondary: platform/product leads and founders (care about TCO, time-to-value, vendor risk, managed vs self-host tradeoffs)

Core positioning thesis (one sentence):
- Redwoods Inference: the predictable inference control plane — same API across hosted, reserved, and private deployments, with token-level observability and rollback-safe rollouts so engineers ship LLM features without guesswork.

Why this slice?
- We believe the decisive purchase trigger is: certainty — predictable tail latency, predictable cost per useful token, and predictable rollback when quality shifts. Marketing lines that promise "speed" or "cost" alone feel commoditized; "predictability" + "control" maps to developer procurement.

Hero copy experiments (3 orthogonal axes to test)
- Axis A: Assertive technical hook (SLO-first)
  - Variant A1 (short): "Inference you can SLA: predictable latency, predictable cost."
  - Variant A2 (long): "Ship LLM features with SLOs you can measure: token-level tracing, canary rollouts, and predictable tail latency."

- Axis B: Economic hook (unit economics)
  - Variant B1: "Cut per-token cost with batching, prefix caching, and smart routing."
  - Variant B2: "Lower inference spend without sacrificing response quality — automatically."

- Axis C: Operational control (parity across environments)
  - Variant C1: "One API across hosted, dedicated, and private — same behavior, same tooling."
  - Variant C2: "Model rollouts and fallbacks across regions and infra, out of the box."

Combo examples (quick reads for hero + subhead):
- Combo 1 (SLO-first):
  - Headline: "Inference you can SLA."
  - Subhead: "Token-level observability, canary rollouts, and fallback policies so your app stays healthy when models drift."
  - CTA: "Start a test run" / "Request a latency report"

- Combo 2 (Economics + dev focus):
  - Headline: "High-throughput inference that pays for itself."
  - Subhead: "Automatic batching, caching, and quantization guidance to cut costs while keeping tail-latency tight."
  - CTA: "Estimate your savings" / "Try cost-optimized endpoint"

Hero microcopy rules (keep consistent):
- Use verbs that imply control: measure, pin, rollback, route, canary, fall back.
- Avoid generic adjectives alone (fast/cheap) without the mechanism. Always follow with "how" in a second line.
- Where possible add a concrete unit (ms, % of tokens saved, cost $/k tokens) — these will be swapped with live metrics in experiments.

Key trust signals and placement (ordered approximate priority for engineering buyer):
1) Inline latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) by workload example (small code snippet near hero or above fold)
2) Model catalog + benchmark short-cards (which model family, token cost, context length)
3) Diagram: runtime -> compiler -> kernel selection -> routing -> fallback (keep to 1 row of icons + 1 sentence each)
4) Customer logos (engineering-centric: product logos with a one-line anecdote)
5) Short quote from SRE/ML engineer on SLA example (not marketing speak)
6) Link to reproducible benchmark repo and cost calculator (opens GitHub/Playbook)

Competitive framing (notes for comparison panel / positioning copy):
- Frame: "Why not build? Why not use X?" answers.
- Short plays:
  - Against managed endpoints that hide ops: "Managed, but measurable — get metrics you can export and pin to SLAs."
  - Against self-hosted inference stacks: "Less infra burden; same control over routing and configs — also optional private install if you must run in-house."
  - Against low-cost/commodity providers: "Transparent unit economics and tail-latency SLOs, not just a cheap per-token sticker price."

Example comparison blurbs (for a small three-column block):
- Build in-house: "Flexible, but months of infra, no standardized rollback or reproducible performance profiles."
- Commodity API: "Cheap today; unpredictable tail costs and regional failover is ad hoc."
- Redwood Inference: "Predictable throughput, cost-aware controls, and rollout primitives — same API everywhere."

Objection handling snippets (FAQ-style short answers)
- Q: "Can I keep data in our VPC?" A: "Yes — private control plane plus on-prem package and KMS integrations are available."
- Q: "What happens if a model suddenly starts hallucinating?" A: "Canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks keep traffic on a safer variant while you triage; token-level tracing points to the prompt sets that regressed."
- Q: "Is it locked to a single model vendor?" A: "No — model catalog and routing policies make switching or multi-model strategies painless."

Sample product page outline (copy skeleton)
- H1: short variant of hero chosen from experiments
- H2: 2–3 line summary of the operational primitives (routing, caching, rollouts)
- Feature grid: 6 cards with short 12–18 word bullets (examples below)
  - Token-level observability: "Trace costs, latency, and quality at token granularity."
  - Canary deploys & rollbacks: "Safe rollouts with automatic fallback on regressions."
  - Dedicated pools & burst capacity: "Predictable throughput under commit or burst to meet spikes."
  - Model and quantization recommendations: "Workload-driven suggestions to balance quality and cost."
  - Single API, multiple deployment modes: "Switch between hosted, dedicated, or private with the same SDK."
  - Cost tooling & batching: "Automated batching, caching, and a cost estimator for endpoint tuning."

Copy tone guide (short):
- Keep sentences short (12–18 words). Prefer active voice.
- Lean technical but friendly — assume reader understands terms like canary, p95, KV cache.
- When writing for homepage, prioritize a fast scan: 1 H1, 1–2 H2s, 4 trust hooks, 1 CTA.

Experiment matrix (recommended first 6 experiments)
- Exp 1: Hero: "Inference you can SLA" vs "High-throughput inference that pays for itself"
  - Primary metric: click-through to product page; Secondary: demo requests
- Exp 2: Inline p99 numbers shown vs generic claim ("low tail latency")
  - Metric: time-on-site for technical docs; engagement with benchmark repo
- Exp 3: CTA wording: "Start a test run" vs "Estimate your savings"
  - Metric: demo requests vs cost-calculator launches
- Exp 4: Trust panel order (benchmarks first vs logos first)
  - Metric: product page scroll depth and contact conversions
- Exp 5: Feature language: "canary rollouts" vs "safe rollouts"
  - Metric: search term clicks for docs and FAQ usage
- Exp 6: Economics badge with % savings estimate in hero vs no badge
  - Metric: demo requests and quote requests for dedicated

Quantitative targets / success criteria
- Winning hero variant: 10% uplift in product page clicks and 8% uplift in demo signups over 6 weeks.
- Showing p99 numbers: 15% increase in benchmark repo clones or clicks to reproducible tests.

Implementation notes for eng & analytics
- Add event tags: hero_variant, trust_signal_shown, cta_clicked -> wire to amplitude and GA4.
- For inline percentiles, create a small JSON endpoint that returns latest p50/p95/p99 for several canned workloads; cache for 5m.
- Copy team to coordinate with docs: link to benchmark repo and create a short walkthrough README for customers to reproduce tests.

Open questions / decisions to make
- Do we want a continuous live p99 in hero or a static periodic snapshot? (ops cost vs credibility tradeoff)
- Which customer quotes can be tailored for engineering readability? Need SRE-sourced language.
- Should the cost calculator require a login? (friction vs lead quality)

Next steps (short checklist)
- [ ] Pick 3 hero combos to wire up to experiment framework (Carmen + Ethan)
- [ ] Draft smaller microcopy set for feature cards (Priya)
- [ ] Engineering to spec the percentile JSON endpoint and a small benchmark embed (Liam)
- [ ] Legal/Comms to approve customer quotes (Samira)

Notes to self / shorthand for future edits:
- Keep a bin of live metrics and example workloads (chat, codegen, summarization) — swap into hero depending on experiment persona.
- Avoid overpromising SLA names ("SLA-backed") until legal and SRE sign-off.

References and manual links to stitch into page:
- Benchmark repo: github.com/redwood-inference/repro-benchmarks
- Cost estimator: github.com/redwood-inference/cost-estimator (prototype)
- Related Confluence: CONFLUENCE-4521 (GTM messaging repo)

End of draft.

Quick changelog: 2026-03-01 — Reordered trust panel and added experiment matrix; noted open ops question about live percentiles.
